moreFaqs.a: A salary garnishment order is served on the company, so the company learns of the garnishment. Because this is service under a court procedure, it is different from the plaintiff telling the company directly. In many cases, the other party, wanting to avoid this, gets in touch first.

moreFaqs.q: Will the judgment show my name and all the details? Can other people see it?
moreFaqs.a: Written judgments can be viewed by the public, but personal information such as the parties' names is redacted (Civil Procedure Act (민사소송법) Article 163-2). Some details of the case still remain, so if you don't want a written judgment on record, consider ending the case through mediation or settlement.

moreFaqs.q: How are consultation fees and legal fees decided?
moreFaqs.a: We explain the fees after the consultation, once we have heard the details of the case and the scope of work. They depend on whether you are the plaintiff or the defendant, whether the case ends in settlement or goes to trial, and whether procedures such as evidence preservation are needed.

moreFaqs.q: Can I get a consultation at night or on weekends?
moreFaqs.a: You can send us a message through the chat on this page at any time, including weekends and public holidays. Consultations are available at our main office in Seoul and our branch offices in Incheon, Hongseong and Songpa, and you are welcome to message us first and describe your situation before visiting.

moreFaqs.q: Will my spouse or the other party find out what I discussed in the consultation?
moreFaqs.a: Lawyers must not disclose secrets learned in the course of their work (Attorney-at-Law Act (변호사법) Article 26). We do not disclose the fact or content of a consultation to anyone without the client's consent. Consultations are conducted personally by a managing partner. At Jisan Law, we do not hide behind office managers or associate lawyers.

moreFaqs.q: If I lose, do I have to pay the other side's lawyer's fees too?
moreFaqs.a: As a rule, litigation costs are borne by the losing party (Civil Procedure Act (민사소송법) Article 98), and the other side's lawyer's fees are included in litigation costs within the limits set by Supreme Court rules (Article 109 of the same Act). If each side partly wins and partly loses, the court decides the ratio (Article 101 of the same Act).

moreFaqs.q: What should I bring to the consultation?
moreFaqs.a: Bring notes on how you found out about the affair, materials such as screenshots or photos, and whatever you know about the affair partner. If you received a complaint or a certified letter, also bring the envelope and the notice so we can check the deadline right away. It's fine if your materials are not organized.

moreFaqs.category: Infidelity & Affair Lawsuits · Criminal & Workplace Issues
moreFaqs.q: Is it risky even to quietly tell only the HR team at the other woman's company?
moreFaqs.a: Even if you tell only one person, if that person is likely to spread it to others, the publicity element (공연성) of defamation may be recognized. If the purpose is clear, such as asking for the two to be separated at work, and the wording is restrained, there is room to argue, but the outcome is hard to predict. Before telling anyone, first consider blocking contact through mediation in the affair lawsuit or a settlement agreement.

moreFaqs.category: Infidelity & Affair Lawsuits · Criminal & Workplace Issues
moreFaqs.q: The affair partner is demanding money, saying, 'I'll tell your spouse everything.'
moreFaqs.a: Demanding money under threat of exposure can amount to extortion (공갈) or threats (협박). Do not send money, and keep the messages and call records of the demand exactly as they are. If the contact is repeated or they come to see you, you can also report it as stalking.

moreFaqs.category: Infidelity & Affair Lawsuits · Criminal & Workplace Issues
moreFaqs.q: I'm the defendant in an affair lawsuit, and my company says it will discipline me.
moreFaqs.a: An affair is a private matter, so on its own it is hard to see as a legitimate ground for discipline. However, if it disrupted work or risked harming the company's reputation, discipline may be upheld. What you say in the disciplinary process can also affect the affair lawsuit, so prepare your written explanation in advance before submitting it.

moreFaqs.q: Can I put a recorder in my spouse's car to catch evidence of the affair?
moreFaqs.a: Recording a conversation you are not part of is a crime under the Protection of Communications Secrets Act (통신비밀보호법) that carries imprisonment with no fine option. On April 30, 2026, the Supreme Court held that a recording obtained this way is not admissible as evidence even in a lawsuit for affair compensation (2024다222212). You would bear the risk of punishment and still be unable to use it as evidence, so find another way.

moreFaqs.q: Is it okay to secretly install a location-sharing app on my spouse's phone?
moreFaqs.a: Collecting someone's location information without their consent can be punished under the Location Information Act (위치정보법) with up to 3 years' imprisonment or a fine of up to KRW 30 million. This applies between spouses as well. If you need their movements, first look for material that can be obtained through court procedures, such as card payment records or CCTV at lodging businesses.

moreFaqs.category: Infidelity & Affair Lawsuits · Responding as Defendant
moreFaqs.q: Do I have to prove that the couple was already separated at the time?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. Under Supreme Court case law, the affair partner who argues that the marriage had already broken down beyond repair at the time of the infidelity must prove it (Supreme Court Decision 2022므13504, 13511, rendered June 27, 2024). Rather than what the other person's spouse told you, you need objective material such as records of a divorce filing or a change of address.

moreFaqs.q: My husband's affair partner is also married. What happens if her husband sues my husband?
moreFaqs.a: Your lawsuit against the other woman and her husband's lawsuit against your husband proceed separately, and each gets its own judgment. If both couples stay married, money can end up going in and out of the same household, so sometimes the parties settle by agreeing not to make claims against each other and only promising no contact and confidentiality.

moreFaqs.q: The other woman says she is pregnant with my husband's child. Does this affect the compensation?
moreFaqs.a: Pregnancy or the birth of a child outside the marriage can be considered when setting compensation, as a circumstance showing that the infidelity was serious. However, the amount is decided case by case, looking also at the length of the marriage, the length of the relationship and whether there is a divorce. You also need to sort out whether the pregnancy claim is true and how acknowledgment of paternity (인지) and child support will be handled.

moreFaqs.q: How long does it take to get a result after I file a renunciation of inheritance?
moreFaqs.a: If there is nothing wrong with the documents, the written decision accepting it usually comes within 1 to 2 months after filing. It can take longer depending on the court's workload or if you receive an order to correct (보정명령). The deadline only requires that your filing is received in time, so waiting for the result does not put you at a disadvantage.

moreFaqs.q: Do I have to report the death before I can renounce the inheritance?
moreFaqs.a: The filing must include documents such as the deceased's basic certificate (기본증명서) and resident registration abstract of a deregistered person (말소자 주민등록초본), so in practice you file after the death has been reported. The death must be reported within 1 month from the day you learned of it.

moreFaqs.q: If I renounce the inheritance, do my children also have to renounce separately?
moreFaqs.a: If the deceased's children renounce while the deceased's spouse is alive, the spouse becomes the sole heir and the grandchildren do not become heirs. If there is no spouse, or the spouse has also renounced, the grandchildren become the next heirs. In that case, either the grandchildren also renounce, or you consider having one person take limited acceptance (한정승인) from the start.

moreFaqs.q: My uncle has died. Could I become his heir?
moreFaqs.a: If your uncle had no spouse, children or parents, and his siblings (such as your parent) are also gone or have all renounced, you as his nephew or niece, a collateral blood relative within the fourth degree, can become an heir. To avoid his debts, you must also renounce or file for limited acceptance within 3 months from the day you learned that everyone ahead of you had renounced.

moreFaqs.q: If I take limited acceptance, can I keep living in the house I inherited?
moreFaqs.a: Limited acceptance is a procedure for paying debts out of the estate. If the house is the only asset and the debts are larger, it often ends up being sold at auction. If you want to keep the house, check in advance whether you can pay creditors an amount equal to the estate's value from your own money.

moreFaqs.q: My parent had overdue credit card debt. Do I inherit the late interest as well?
moreFaqs.a: If you accept the inheritance, you take over the principal, interest and late-payment damages exactly as they are. If you renounce, you take over none of it. If you take limited acceptance, you are liable only up to the value of the estate.

moreFaqs.q: Can renouncing the inheritance also get me out of my parent's unpaid taxes?
moreFaqs.a: The deceased's unpaid national and local taxes are also debts of the estate. If you renounce, as a rule you do not take them over, and if you take limited acceptance, you must pay them only up to the value of the estate. However, if an heir who renounced or took limited acceptance received insurance money because of the death, that money may be treated as inherited property and the heir may have to pay the deceased's national taxes from it (Framework Act on National Taxes (국세기본법) Article 24(2)). Taxes that arise for the heir personally, such as inheritance tax, are a separate matter.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: Where can I see the detailed results of the Safe Inheritance search?
moreFaqs.a: Each agency sends its results by text message, and you check the details on that agency's site: the Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) site for financial accounts, Hometax (the National Tax Service's online portal) for national taxes, each pension service for pensions, and so on. Follow the instructions on your application receipt and print the results from each agency's site. Financial search results can be viewed on the Financial Supervisory Service website only for 3 months from the application date.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: Can I still search the deceased's assets after renouncing the inheritance?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. Searching for assets is not a disposal of estate property, so it does not affect your renunciation. However, the Safe Inheritance One-Stop Service (안심상속 원스톱서비스) must be applied for within 1 year from the last day of the month in which the person died.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: How do I close the deceased's mobile phone and automatic payments?
moreFaqs.a: Notify the mobile carrier of the death and cancel the line. Any remaining charges are treated as a debt of the estate. Automatic payments for utilities and insurance may stop once the account is blocked after the death is reported, so change how they are paid in advance. If you are thinking of renouncing, it is safer not to take new money out of the deceased's account to pay them.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: How do we collect money owed to the deceased, such as loans they made or a lease deposit?
moreFaqs.a: Money owed to the deceased is also part of the estate, so the heirs receive it according to their statutory shares, or the person chosen by agreement receives it. However, if you are thinking of renouncing or taking limited acceptance, collecting and spending it can count as disposing of the estate, so it is safer not to collect it before you decide.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: How are stocks or securities accounts inherited?
moreFaqs.a: The usual way is to submit an agreement signed by all the heirs, or the required documents, to the securities company and move the holdings into an account in the heir's name. Because share prices keep changing, you need to consider both the valuation date for inheritance tax and the timing of the division agreement.

moreFaqs.q: Does an agreement on division of the estate have to be notarized?
moreFaqs.a: Notarization is not required. If every heir stamps it with their registered seal and attaches a certificate of seal impression (인감증명서), it can be used for registration and banking. If an heir lives abroad, a signature certificate or local notarization may be needed.

moreFaqs.q: If one person gets the whole house through a division agreement, is gift tax charged?
moreFaqs.a: Even if the heirs agree to divide the estate differently from the statutory shares, a division made before the first inheritance registration is, as a rule, treated as acquired by inheritance. However, readjusting shares again after registration may be treated as a gift, so timing matters. The specific tax should be checked with a tax accountant.

moreFaqs.q: I want to sell our parents' house and split the money, but one sibling objects.
moreFaqs.a: If you cannot agree, you can ask for division by auction in an adjudication on division of the estate (상속재산분할). If the house has already been registered in your statutory shares and is co-owned, you can also seek an auction through a lawsuit for partition of co-owned property (공유물분할). Which procedure fits depends on the registration status and whether there are special benefit or contribution share issues.

moreFaqs.q: My mother died after my father, before his estate was settled. How does inheritance work?
moreFaqs.a: If your mother died before your father's inheritance was settled, the share she would have received from your father passes in turn to her heirs. The two inheritances must be calculated in order, and in a blended family the heirs may differ, so the first step is to sort out the family relationships.

moreFaqs.q: Who pays the rent or maintenance fees while an adjudication on division of the estate is pending?
moreFaqs.a: Until division, the estate is co-owned, so as a rule the costs of managing it are also shared according to each heir's share. If one person paid on behalf of the others, keep a record of the amounts and ask for them to be settled in the division adjudication.

moreFaqs.q: Are my parent's debts deducted when calculating the forced heirship share?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. The base amount is calculated by taking the property at the date of death, adding the gifts that are counted, and deducting the full amount of the estate's debts (Civil Act (민법) Article 1113). If the debts are large, the forced heirship share (유류분) is reduced accordingly.

moreFaqs.q: My parent donated their entire estate to a charitable organization. Can I claim my forced heirship share?
moreFaqs.a: Even when the recipient of a bequest or gift is an organization rather than an heir, it can be subject to a forced heirship share claim. However, a lifetime gift is only counted if it was made within 1 year before the death, or if both sides knew it would harm the forced heirship share.

moreFaqs.q: If I file a forced heirship share lawsuit, can it end in mediation with my siblings?
moreFaqs.a: Many cases end in mediation during the lawsuit. Once the appraisal results come out and the amount becomes reasonably clear, it is easier to find a figure both sides can accept. Payment in installments or how to arrange shares in real estate can also be decided in mediation.

moreFaqs.q: I have received a forced heirship share claim. Can I still sell the house?
moreFaqs.a: Unless it is legally blocked, you can sell it, but selling during the lawsuit may lead to a provisional injunction or weaken your position in negotiations. For inheritances that began on or after March 17, 2026, the rule is to return value in money, so the issue becomes raising the amount to be returned rather than the sale itself.

moreFaqs.q: Can a grandchild who inherits by representation also claim a forced heirship share?
moreFaqs.a: If your parent died first and you became your grandparent's heir by representation (대습상속), you can take over and claim the forced heirship share your parent would have had. If there are several siblings, you divide your parent's share among you.

moreFaqs.q: Does a will have to be notarized?
moreFaqs.a: No. A will is valid without notarization if it meets the requirements for a handwritten will (자필증서 유언). However, a handwritten will needs a court inspection (검인) after the death and easily leads to disputes over the handwriting or mental capacity, so if a dispute is expected, a notarized will (공정증서 유언) is recommended.

moreFaqs.q: Who becomes the executor of a will?
moreFaqs.a: The executor can be named in the will, or the will can leave the choice to a third party. If no one is named, the heirs become the executors, and the family court appoints one if needed. Naming a neutral person who is not receiving property reduces disputes during execution.

moreFaqs.q: Can a parent who has been diagnosed with dementia still make a will?
moreFaqs.a: A diagnosis alone does not take away the capacity to make a will. The test is whether, at the time of the will, the person could understand and judge their own property and the content of the will. A person under adult guardianship can make a will when their mental capacity has recovered, and a doctor must record that condition in the will and sign and seal it (Civil Act Article 1063).

moreFaqs.q: Can a will include a condition like 'you get the house if you take care of me'?
moreFaqs.a: This can be set up as a bequest with a burden. If the recipient does not carry out the burden, the heirs or the executor can set a period and demand performance, and if it is still not performed, they can ask the court to revoke the will (Civil Act Article 1111).

moreFaqs.q: How long does a lawsuit to invalidate a will take?
moreFaqs.a: Handwriting analysis or a court-ordered review of medical records is often needed, so the first instance alone commonly takes around a year. Meanwhile, you must keep track of the deadline for a forced heirship share claim so it does not pass.

moreFaqs.q: Does a partner who never registered the marriage inherit?
moreFaqs.a: A de facto spouse (common-law partner) is not an heir. Only when there are no other heirs at all can they ask, as a person with a special relationship to the deceased, to be granted part of the estate, and this must be done within 2 months after the public notice period searching for heirs ends (Civil Act Article 1057-2).

moreFaqs.q: Does a divorced former spouse inherit?
moreFaqs.a: After a divorce, the person is no longer a spouse and has no inheritance rights. However, children born to the former couple are heirs as children, regardless of their parents' divorce.

moreFaqs.q: Can a child born outside marriage inherit?
moreFaqs.a: If the father acknowledged the child or there is a court judgment of acknowledgment, the child has the same share as any other child. If the acknowledgment came after the estate was already divided, the child can claim payment of the value of their share of the divided estate (Civil Act Article 1014). This claim must be made within 3 years from the day the child learned of the infringement. However, on June 27, 2024, the Constitutional Court ruled the 10-years-from-infringement limit unconstitutional (2021헌마1588), so the claim is not barred merely because the estate was divided long ago.

moreFaqs.q: What happens if a person who would have been an heir died first?
moreFaqs.a: If a child or sibling died before the deceased, that person's lineal descendants and spouse inherit in their place (inheritance by representation, 대습상속). A daughter-in-law or son-in-law can become an heir this way. When an heir is disqualified or has been declared to have lost inheritance rights, their lineal descendants still inherit by representation, but under the Civil Act as amended on March 17, 2026, the spouse cannot inherit by representation in that case (Articles 1001 and 1003(2)).

moreFaqs.a: We explain the fees after the consultation, once we have looked at the type and scope of the case. Work with a set procedure, like filing a renunciation of inheritance, differs greatly from lawsuits such as forced heirship share claims or division adjudications, where appraisals and inquiries follow one after another.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Fees and Hiring a Lawyer
moreFaqs.q: Can my siblings and I hire you together?
moreFaqs.a: Several heirs in the same position can hire us together. However, if the heirs' interests conflict on some points, one lawyer may not be able to represent both sides, so we check this first in the consultation.

moreFaqs.q: My father, who is still alive, says he has a lot of debt and wants me to renounce the inheritance in advance. Can I do that now?
moreFaqs.a: No. Renunciation of inheritance only takes effect if it is filed with the family court after the inheritance begins, that is, after the death, within 3 months from the day you learned that the inheritance began (Civil Act Articles 1019 and 1041). A written promise to renounce made while he is alive, or documents filed in advance, will not protect you from the debts, so you must file again within the deadline after his death.

moreFaqs.q: If I renounce because of my dad's debts, will my credit rating drop? Will I lose access to student loans?
moreFaqs.a: Renunciation means you never inherit the deceased's debts in the first place, so renouncing does not cause the deceased's debts to be recorded as yours. However, if you acted as a guarantor for the deceased's loan, or took out a loan jointly with them, that part remains your debt regardless of the renunciation. First check whether there are any guarantor documents.

moreFaqs.q: My renunciation has been accepted. What should I do with my father's wallet and cash that the hospital gave me?
moreFaqs.a: Do not spend it; keep it as it is. A person who renounced must continue to manage the estate until the person who became heir because of the renunciation can manage it (Civil Act Article 1044). Write down the date and amount you received, and hand it over once the next heir is determined. Spending this money could be treated as wrongful use after renunciation.

moreFaqs.q: Does a baby who was in the mother's womb at the time of death also need to renounce?
moreFaqs.a: For inheritance purposes, an unborn child is treated as already born and becomes an heir (Civil Act Article 1000(3)). So even if the whole family renounces, the baby's share must be handled separately, and after the birth the parent with parental authority files the renunciation or limited acceptance on the child's behalf. If the parent's and the child's interests conflict, a special representative (특별대리인) may be needed, and the deadline must be worked out case by case, so get advice right after the birth.

moreFaqs.category: Inheritance · Asset Search and Bank Deposits
moreFaqs.q: My birth mother, whom I had no contact with, has died, and the one-stop search does not work for me. How can I find out her assets and debts?
moreFaqs.a: The Safe Inheritance One-Stop Service must be applied for within 1 year from the last day of the month of death, and online applications through Government24 (the government's online portal) are open only to first- and second-ranked heirs. If the period has passed or the online route is blocked, visit a community service center (주민센터), or apply separately for the Financial Supervisory Service's inquiry into an heir's financial transactions. You apply for that inquiry at the Financial Supervisory Service, a bank, a post office or similar, submitting the basic certificate (or death certificate), a family relationship certificate based on the deceased, and your ID. Results usually come within 20 days and can be viewed on the website for 3 months from the application date.

moreFaqs.q: I heard the forced heirship share for siblings was ruled unconstitutional. Does that mean I, as a child, can no longer file a forced heirship share claim?
moreFaqs.a: No. The 2024 Constitutional Court decision abolished only the forced heirship share of the deceased's siblings. Children and spouses still have a forced heirship share of one half of their statutory share, and parents one third. However, some things have changed for inheritances that began on or after March 17, 2026: as a rule, value is returned in money, and gifts received in return for specially supporting a parent may be excluded from the calculation to that extent. Start by checking the date of death.

moreFaqs.q: I heard that once 10 years have passed since a gift, you can no longer claim a forced heirship share. Is that true?
moreFaqs.a: This is commonly confused. The 10 years for a forced heirship share run not from the date of the gift but from the date the inheritance began, that is, the date of death (Civil Act Article 1117). Also, under case law, gifts received by co-heirs are counted even if they were made long ago. The 10-year look-back for gifts is part of the inheritance tax calculation, which is a different matter. What you should check first is the much shorter period of 1 year from the day you learned of the gift or bequest.

moreFaqs.q: To put the house in our mother's name, do we children have to renounce the inheritance? Would that also mean renouncing our mother's estate later?
moreFaqs.a: A renunciation applies only to this inheritance from your father and has nothing to do with the inheritance when your mother dies in the future. However, to give the house to your mother, a division by agreement, in which all the heirs sign an agreement and the house is registered in your mother's name alone, is more common than renunciation. Renunciation also settles the debts and cannot be undone, so decide after looking at whether there are debts and at the taxes.

moreFaqs.q: Is there a fine if we put off inheritance registration for several years?
moreFaqs.a: No provision sets a deadline for inheritance registration itself, so registering late does not lead to a fine. However, acquisition tax must be reported within 6 months from the last day of the month in which the inheritance began (9 months if an heir has an address abroad), and a penalty tax is added after that (Local Tax Act (지방세법) Article 20). Also keep in mind that if another heir dies while you wait, more people will be involved in sorting it out.

moreFaqs.q: We decided to sell the inherited house and split the money. Whose bank account should receive the sale price?
moreFaqs.a: All the co-heirs are sellers, so the rule is that each receives the price according to their share. If you agree that one person's account will receive it and then divide it, put that agreement in writing, including the settlement date and amounts. If the person who received the money does not settle up, that document becomes the basis for a claim to get it back.

moreFaqs.q: My family member died in a workplace accident. Do the heirs split the survivor benefits?
moreFaqs.a: They are not split according to inheritance shares. Industrial accident survivor benefits are paid in the order set by law: first the spouse, children, parents, grandchildren and grandparents who shared a household with the worker at the time of death, and if several people are in the same rank, they share equally (Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act (산업재해보상보험법) Article 65). If the worker designated a recipient by will, that designation is followed.

moreFaqs.q: Does my half-sibling inherit from our father on the same terms as me?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. All of your father's children have the same rank and the same share, regardless of who their mother is (Civil Act Article 1009(1)). A child born outside marriage becomes an heir only after the father registers an acknowledgment or there is a court judgment of acknowledgment.

moreFaqs.q: Are the debts from my father's shop also inherited? Is closing the shop enough?
moreFaqs.a: The business debts of a sole proprietor are your father's personal debts, so they are inherited as they are. Closing the shop does not make the debts disappear, so if you do not know how large they are, consider limited acceptance or renunciation within 3 months. Disposing of stock or equipment while winding up can be treated as simple acceptance (단순승인), so be careful about the order of steps.

moreFaqs.q: My mother gave my older brother a house. Can I challenge it while she is still alive?
moreFaqs.a: The forced heirship share and inheritance shares can only be claimed after the inheritance begins, so it is hard for another child to directly challenge the gift while your mother is alive. If your mother was not in a state to make sound decisions at the time of the gift, she herself or her guardian can claim the gift is invalid. For now, the realistic step is to gather materials showing how the gift came about and your mother's condition.

moreFaqs.q: If I become my parent's adult guardian, can I use their money for my travel costs or as payment for my effort?
moreFaqs.a: A guardian may use the parent's property only for the parent's benefit. Whether the guardian is paid is decided by the family court on the guardian's request, based on the parent's financial situation (Civil Act Article 955). Do not take money on your own, and keep records and receipts of all spending.

moreFaqs.q: If I file a criminal complaint against a sibling who took money from the deceased's account, will I also get the money back?
moreFaqs.a: Criminal proceedings decide whether someone is punished. To get the money back, you need a separate civil procedure, such as a claim for its return or a division of the estate. Transaction records confirmed during the investigation can be used as evidence in the civil case, and the other side sometimes offers to settle.

moreFaqs.q: If my parent sold the house named in their will while they were alive, what happens to the will?
moreFaqs.a: If, after making a will, a person does something during their lifetime that conflicts with it, that part of the will is treated as revoked (Civil Act Article 1109). If the house was sold, the gift of that house in the will has no effect, and whether the beneficiary can receive the sale proceeds instead must be examined separately based on the wording of the will.
